carrots-fresh-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-to-.title: Carrots, fresh, cooked, fat added, NS as to fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Carrot (Daucus carota) is a root vegetable widely used in cooking. Fresh carrots are crisp and mildly sweet, while cooking softens them. When prepared with added fat (oil, butter) they gain a richer flavor and higher energy content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots were among the first cultivated crops over 5,000 years ago.
The orange color was popularized by Dutch breeders in the 17th century.
More than 100 varieties exist, ranging from purple and yellow to red and white.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Raw carrot sticks are a common healthy snack.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in carrots converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Fiber and antioxidants help lower cholesterol and protect blood vessels.

items.title: Potassium content
items.content: Potassium aids normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Low calorie (without fat)
items.content: Fresh carrots are low in calories, making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Excess beta‑carotene
items.content: Very high intake can cause carotenemia – a harmless yellowing of the skin.

items.title: Contamination during processing
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial growth, especially in cooked carrots with added fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh carrots are eaten raw in salads, juices, or as snacks. Cooked carrots are used in soups, purees, and side dishes. Adding fat allows sautéing, braising or roasting with oil, butter or other fats for enhanced flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh carrots in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or vegetable drawer – up to 2 weeks. Cooked carrots with fat should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3‑4 days. Discard if off‑smell or mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Crackers are dry baked snacks, usually made from wheat or rye flour, often seasoned with salt and oil. Milk is a nutrient‑rich liquid produced by the mammary glands of mammals, containing proteins, fats, vitamins, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers originated in Europe in the 19th century as a durable, portable food.
There are over 200 varieties of crackers, ranging from plain salty to sweet with seeds and spices.
Milk serves as the base for more than 1,000 products, including cheese, yogurt, and ice cream.
In many cultures milk is consumed as fermented drinks such as kefir and ayran.
Crackers are frequently used as a base for canapés and appetizers.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Crackers provide quickly digestible carbs that supply energy.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Milk is one of the best dietary sources of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk contains vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and vitamin B12, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Milk delivers complete protein with all essential amino acids.

items.title: Probiotics (in fermented dairy)
items.content: Fermented milk drinks provide beneficial bacteria that promote gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Some people lack sufficient lactase enzyme, leading to discomfort after drinking milk.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey can cause severe reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Certain crackers are high in salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Both crackers and whole milk can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed plain, paired with cheese, pâtés, or dips. Milk is drunk on its own, added to coffee, cereals, smoothies, or used in cooking and baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place to keep them crisp. Milk should be kept refrigerated at 2‑4 °C and consumed before the expiration date on the package.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white is the clear part of the egg, composed almost entirely of proteins and a small amount of minerals. When cooked with a little added fat (e.g., oil or butter) it becomes more flavorful and slightly more caloric, while still remaining low‑fat compared with the yolk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is about 90 % water and 10 % proteins, the main one being albumin.
Heat causes protein denaturation, making the white firm and easily digestible.
Adding a modest amount of fat (1‑2 g) improves taste and helps absorb any fat‑soluble vitamins present in the dish.
In 1944 the USDA assigned code 1944 to cooked egg white with added fat in the national nutrient database.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A typical serving (≈30 g) provides about 4 g of complete protein, essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Without added fat, egg white contains virtually no saturated fat; even with a small amount of added fat the overall fat content remains low.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Egg white supplies selenium, a trace mineral that supports antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Proteins such as ovalbumin contribute to the synthesis of immunoglobulins.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: One portion of cooked white with a little added fat contains roughly 55 kcal, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Overcooking
items.content: Excessive heating makes the white rubbery and can reduce the bioavailability of certain amino acids.

items.title: Cross‑contamination with yolk
items.content: When prepared together with yolk, cholesterol from the yolk can transfer, which matters for low‑cholesterol diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked egg white with added fat can be sliced into salads, used as a sandwich filling, incorporated into yolk‑free omelets, or blended into protein smoothies. Add 1‑2 tsp of vegetable oil or butter for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it keeps for about 2 months, though texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Lettuce is a salad made from lettuce leaves with assorted vegetables, including tomatoes and/or carrots, served without dressing. It is rich in vitamins, minerals, and fiber, making it a light and nutritious option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lettuce salads are commonly served as a basic side dish in many restaurants.
Tomatoes add bright flavor and lycopene, while carrots provide beta‑carotene.
No dressing preserves the natural taste of fresh vegetables.
Lettuce leaves are a good source of vitamin K, important for blood clotting.
The salad can be easily customized with seasonal vegetables.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The salad provides vitamins A, C, K, and folate, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Its low calorie content makes it suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and beta‑carotene from carrots help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium in the salad helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Vegetable allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to tomatoes or carrots.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw vegetables can harbor salmonella; thorough washing is recommended.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Choose organic produce or wash well to reduce pesticide exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad immediately after preparation to retain its crisp texture. A pinch of salt, pepper, or a squeeze of lemon juice can be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Leaves may lose crunch, so it is best to assemble just before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: The tuna salad sandwich on wheat is a hearty sandwich made with whole‑grain wheat bread, canned tuna, fresh vegetables (usually lettuce, tomato and cucumber) and a light sauce such as mayo or yogurt. It combines fish protein, whole‑grain fiber and vegetable vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the most popular sources of omega‑3 fatty acids in the diet.
Whole‑grain wheat bread retains most of the bran and germ, boosting its fiber content.
Tuna sandwiches are a common component of school lunches in the US and Japan because they are convenient and nutritious.
Canned tuna is usually packed in its own juice or olive oil, which influences flavor and calorie count.
The combination of tuna and fresh veggies helps maintain hydration thanks to the high water content of the vegetables.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: One sandwich delivers about 20‑25 g of protein, aiding muscle repair and satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna and whole‑grain bread supply B12, niacin and folate.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread and vegetables add soluble and insoluble fiber, improving digestion.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Tuna contains selenium, magnesium and potassium, important for metabolism and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tuna.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt, so low‑sodium versions are preferable for those monitoring sodium intake.

items.title: Mercury risk
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for children and pregnant people.

items.title: Bread quality
items.content: Bread high in sugar or trans fats can diminish the sandwich’s overall healthfulness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the sandwich in half and serve immediately after assembly to prevent soggy bread. Add mustard, lemon juice or fresh herbs for extra flavor. It’s easy to pack for on‑the‑go meals in a food‑safe container.

content.title: Storage
content.content: If prepared ahead, keep the sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store bread separate from the filling to avoid sogginess. Unopened canned tuna can be stored in a sealed jar until its expiration date.

turkey-prepackaged-or-deli-luncheon-meat.title: Turkey, prepackaged or deli, luncheon meat

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey deli meat is a ready‑to‑eat sliced product made from turkey, sold either in sealed packages or at the deli counter. It has a mild flavor, light pink color, and a tender texture, suitable for sandwiches, salads, and snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey contains less fat than traditional pork or beef lunch meats.
It is often chosen for diet plans because of its low calorie density.
The product can be smoked, boiled, or baked depending on the processing method.
In many countries it is marketed as “deli turkey” and used as a ham alternative.
Some varieties are fortified with B‑vitamins and zinc.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Turkey provides less saturated fat than many other processed meats, supporting heart‑healthy eating.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A typical serving supplies about 20 g of complete protein, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin, vitamin B6 and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides zinc and selenium, nutrients that support immune function.

items.title: Low calorie count
items.content: One slice (≈30 g) contains roughly 45 kcal, making it convenient for weight control.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain brands add salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some products contain nitrites or other preservatives; those sensitive should avoid them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey deli meat works well in sandwiches, wraps, salads, and as a topping for omelets or pizza. It can be briefly warmed in a pan or microwave if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in the original packaging in the refrigerator at +2–+6 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Freezing is possible for up to 3 months, though texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Waffle is a light, crisp baked good made from a batter of flour, eggs, milk and sugar. Waffles are often served with tea or coffee and can be enjoyed as a snack or used in desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Waffles originated in medieval Europe and were originally cooked in special iron presses.
There are more than 30 types of waffle batters, including Belgian, American and Liege waffles.
Waffles are a common quick and nutritious snack in school cafeterias.
Traditional Belgian waffles have deeper pockets that hold syrup and whipped cream.
Waffles can be sweet or savory depending on the added ingredients.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Waffles provide quickly digestible carbs that give energy for studying and physical activity.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Thanks to eggs and milk, waffles supply a modest amount of both animal and plant protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain batter is enriched with B1, B2 and niacin, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Milk in the batter provides calcium needed for bone growth in children.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture makes waffles convenient for younger children.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet waffles can contain high amounts of sugar, increasing the risk of cavities and excess weight.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional waffles are made with wheat flour, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Cooking in oil high in trans fats can make waffles less healthy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Waffles are relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Waffles can be enjoyed hot with honey, jam, butter or fresh fruit. They are also used in desserts—as a base for cakes, parfaits and ice‑cream toppings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store waffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator up to a week or freeze up to 2 months.
